title: Limpopo River Valley, Mozambique
subtitle: A 12-Day Surface Transformation Along an Irrigated Corridor

processing.window: 30 km x 30 km subset over Chókwè (rows 8870:11870, cols 15321:18321 at 10 m spacing, EPSG:32736, Easting 482975-512975 m, Northing 7272095-7302095 m)
processing.method: Averaged linear power (covariance diagonal) over 6x6 pixel blocks (60 m output posting) before converting to dB; stretched using combined 2nd-98th percentiles (-19.47 to -4.16 dB for HH; -25.03 to -11.62 dB for HV) applied identically to before and after images
processing.access: streamed from ASF Earthdata Cloud (earthaccess + fsspec + h5py), not fully downloaded

sources.name: NASA / ISRO via ASF DAAC
sources.title: NISAR L2 GCOV Provisional Data (Track 114, Frame 165, 2026-01-05 & 2026-01-17)

experiences.title: The Encounter
experiences.place_label: Chókwè Agricultural Corridor, Gaza Province, Mozambique
experiences.hook_question: Between January 5 and January 17, 2026, a broad dark corridor appeared along this river valley and across nearby rectangular fields. What caused such a sudden shift in radar brightness?
experiences.context: The Chókwè region sits along the lower Limpopo River in southern Mozambique, characterized by a winding main channel, oxbow lakes, and a large irrigated agricultural scheme with rectangular field blocks. On its scheduled 12-day repeat orbit, NISAR's L-band radar penetrated cloud cover to capture the ground before and after a dramatic surface shift.

facts.label: Scene Window
facts.value: 30 km × 30 km (3,000 × 3,000 pixels at 10 m spacing)

sar.dialogue: Hello! Welcome to the lower Limpopo River valley in southern Mozambique. Something dramatic altered this landscape in just twelve days—and my L-band radar caught every detail right through the clouds.

experiences.title: The Discovery
experiences.instruction: Drag the Before / After slider to compare January 5 and January 17, switch between HH and HV polarizations, and inspect the brightness change map.

before.caption: Baseline surface conditions on January 5, 2026. The winding river channel appears as a narrow dark ribbon, while surrounding fields and settlements return moderate gray backscatter.

after.caption: Post-event observation on January 17, 2026. A wide dark swath flanks the river channel and fills geometric agricultural blocks in the southeast.

change_map.legend: Red: brighter in the BEFORE image (sharp drop in radar brightness). Cyan: brighter in the AFTER image. Gray/white: little change. Black: no data.
change_map.note: Compares relative radar backscatter brightness (dB), not direct water depth or physical extent.

hotspots.label: Winding River Corridor
hotspots.description: A broad dark band flanks the main channel on January 17, appearing bright red in both HH and HV change maps.

hotspots.label: Southeastern Rectangular Plots
hotspots.description: Geometric irrigated farm blocks shifted sharply from moderate gray to dark in both polarizations.

hotspots.label: Southwestern Permanent Water
hotspots.description: Existing lakes remain dark in both passes, showing near-zero change (gray/black) in the difference map.

sar.dialogue: Slide between January 5 and January 17! Notice how a wide dark corridor suddenly appears along the river bends and fills those rectangular farm plots to the southeast.

experiences.title: The Challenge
experiences.question: Based on the sharp drop in radar brightness along the river channel and across low-lying agricultural plots, what caused this surface change?
hints: Look at the geometry of the bright red zone in the change map: it closely hugs the winding Limpopo River valley and flat irrigation blocks.
Calm open water acts like a mirror to radar pulses, reflecting microwave energy away from the satellite so the surface looks dark.

responses.correct: Spot on! Standing floodwater replaced rough soil and crops with a smooth surface that reflected NISAR's radar pulses away from the antenna, creating that sharp brightness drop (shown in red).
responses.wrong: Interesting hypothesis! Look closely at the geometry of the red zone: it hugs the winding Limpopo River and fills flat rectangular farm plots—a classic signature of standing floodwater creating a smooth, mirror-like surface.

sar.dialogue: Now that you have inspected the before-and-after radar imagery, what event do you think reshaped this river valley?

experiences.title: The Explanation

reveal.summary: Overflow along the Limpopo River inundated surrounding agricultural fields around Chókwè between January 5 and January 17, 2026. Standing water replaced rough soil and crops with a smooth surface that reflected NISAR's L-band radar pulses away from the sensor, producing the wide dark swath on January 17 and the bright red corridor in the change map.

metrics.label: Mean HH Backscatter
metrics.value: Shifted from -11.98 dB (2026-01-05) to -10.90 dB (2026-01-17) across the 30 km window

metrics.label: Mean HV Backscatter
metrics.value: Shifted from -18.83 dB (2026-01-05) to -18.40 dB (2026-01-17) across the 30 km window

experiences.what_radar_sees: Radar transmits microwave pulses and measures the energy scattered back to the satellite. Dry soil and crops scatter energy in many directions (moderate gray brightness), whereas calm floodwater acts like a smooth mirror (specular reflection), bouncing the radar beam away so inundated areas appear very dark.

polarization_expected.text: In SAR literature, co-polarized HH typically provides strong contrast between rough land and smooth open water, while cross-polarized HV is primarily sensitive to volume scattering from vegetation canopies and drops when low crops are submerged.

polarization_observed.text: In our Chókwè GCOV pair, both HH and HV dropped sharply along the Limpopo River corridor and inside the southeastern rectangular agricultural plots (appearing bright red in both change maps), while permanent water bodies in the southwest remained dark in both passes.

how_nisar_detected_it.polarization_note: We report the observed brightness changes in both HH and HV for this specific Provisional GCOV image pair without generalizing them into a universal classification rule, and we do not convert brightness differences directly into floodwater area.

experiences.limitations: This analysis uses PROVISIONAL (Beta) NISAR L2 GCOV data where absolute radiometric calibration is still maturing. Broad cyan brightening outside the river valley (raising scene-wide mean HH by ~1.08 dB) may reflect increased soil moisture after rainfall or provisional calibration differences and cannot be separated without ground validation.

sar.dialogue: Here is the science behind what you saw: calm standing water acts like a mirror to L-band microwaves, bouncing the signal away from my antenna so flooded fields turn dark.

take_action.scenario: You are supporting emergency coordination in Gaza Province on January 17, 2026, with this NISAR brightness change map in hand. What is your next step?

choices.text: Prioritize aerial and field reconnaissance along the red river corridor and southeastern Chókwè farm plots while cross-checking road elevation data.
choices.feedback: Smart decision! Using the radar change map to target reconnaissance—rather than treating it as a standalone damage map—helps response teams focus quickly on the most likely inundated zones.

choices.text: Publish the red pixels directly as an exact street-by-street structural damage map.
choices.feedback: Careful: radar brightness change shows where surface scattering shifted, not structural damage or exact water depth, and provisional data requires ground confirmation.

choices.text: Wait several days for completely cloud-free optical satellite imagery before alerting local teams.
choices.feedback: Waiting for clear skies costs critical response time during storm systems when L-band radar already highlights major corridor changes.

summary.what_happened: River overflow inundated low-lying agricultural plots along the Limpopo River near Chókwè between January 5 and January 17, 2026.
summary.what_nisar_observed: A sharp drop in both HH and HV radar backscatter along the river valley and geometric farm blocks, captured through cloud cover on a 12-day repeat pass.
key_takeaways: L-band radar penetrates storm clouds day and night, revealing river overflow when optical satellites are blocked.
Averaging linear power over 6x6 blocks before dB conversion reduces speckle noise while preserving exact grid alignment.
Brightness change maps highlight where surface scattering changed dramatically, but require local validation before estimating exact flood extent or damage.
summary.looking_forward: As NISAR transitions from provisional to calibrated science operations with regular 12-day global coverage, consistent dual-polarization L-band time series will help hydrologists and disaster agencies monitor major river basins more reliably.

sar.dialogue: Case solved! Radar gives responders an early map of where to look first—even beneath storm clouds. Ready to explore another event on the globe?

caveat: Processed from PROVISIONAL (Beta) NISAR L2 GCOV data; change maps compare relative backscatter brightness (dB) and do not directly measure flood extent, water depth, or structural damage.
